title: Serving patterns: when is a prediction needed?
lead: Select the interaction pattern from the decision’s timing and failure behavior.
bullets: Batch: compute many predictions; consumers read stored results later.
Synchronous: the caller waits for a result during its request.
Asynchronous: an event producer and consumer are decoupled through messaging.
Edge: a deployment location, independent of prediction timing.
example: The churn campaign can use precomputed scores. An immediate fraud check motivates a different timing need.
takeaway: Timing, location, and release strategy are separate choices.

title: Batch serving: validate, score, publish
lead: A complete validated batch must be available before its business deadline.
bullets: Snapshot: define population, cutoff, and required source freshness.
Validate: reject incompatible inputs before scoring.
Reconcile: account for written, rejected, and withheld records.
Publish: expose a validated batch under a defined consumer contract.
example: Monthly churn scores are saved for the campaign. A real numerical deadline must be agreed with campaign owners.
takeaway: Optimize the whole batch deadline, not only per-record prediction speed.

title: Synchronous serving: the caller waits
lead: Prediction becomes part of the application’s response path.
bullets: Response time includes lookup, preparation, inference, and network work.
Availability now affects the waiting application’s request.
Failure behavior needs explicit timeout, error, and fallback policies.
Consistency still requires compatible feature meanings and model versions.
example: An immediate fraud check can justify this pattern. The monthly churn campaign does not require it.
takeaway: A fast model does not guarantee a fast end-to-end service.

title: Asynchronous serving: decouple the work
lead: Messages separate production, processing, and consumption of a prediction.
bullets: Buffering absorbs bursts and supports independent processing.
Lag and queue health become operational concerns.
Retries require failure handling and idempotent processing.
Contracts define message identity, timing, schema, and result interpretation.
example: If a future campaign consumes prediction events, a repeated message must not cause duplicate customer contacts.
takeaway: Decoupling adds messaging responsibilities; it does not remove timing requirements.

title: Deployment location is a separate decision
lead: Central, embedded, and edge deployments change operations and constraints.
bullets: Central: simplify shared operation and governance.
Embedded: deploy the model with its host application.
Edge: account for constrained hardware and intermittent connectivity.
Choose independently: location does not uniquely determine batch or request timing.
example: Keep churn centrally governed. Device-local inference is a contrast, not an extra subsystem to implement here.

title: Package the whole compatible set
lead: A deployable release contains more than the learned model file.
bullets: Model artifact: the learned parameters and required format.
Runtime: dependencies, preparation code, and execution environment.
Contract: feature meaning, types, missingness, and temporal cutoff.
Configuration: scoring population and execution settings.
example: The bank packages M1 with the exact feature interpretation needed to score the monthly customer snapshot.
takeaway: A package that loads successfully still needs release and quality evidence.

title: Shadow deployment: observe without acting
lead: A candidate scores real inputs while the approved model remains the action source.
bullets: Run in parallel against comparable production inputs.
Record identity: distinguish M1 and M2 outputs explicitly.
Compare operational behavior and score differences first.
Wait for labels to compare future churn quality.
example: Only the M1 record is eligible for campaign use; M2’s shadow score cannot create a second offer.
takeaway: Shadow checks observation, not the business effect of acting on the candidate.

title: Canary deployment: limit exposure
lead: An approved limited cohort uses the candidate before broader rollout.
bullets: Restrict exposure to a defined cohort and scope.
Observe execution, compatibility, coverage, and policy behavior.
Define stop rules and a rehearsed recovery path.
Separate evidence: short operational success cannot prove 30-day predictive quality.
example: The bank may authorize a small cohort to use M2 while retaining M1 for the remainder.
takeaway: A canary controls risk; it is not automatically a valid business experiment.

title: A/B testing: define the intervention
lead: Assigned groups and a stated outcome make the comparison interpretable.
bullets: State what changes: model, decision policy, or retention treatment.
Assign comparable groups under an appropriate experiment design.
Define outcomes and the observation window before interpreting results.
Avoid confounding: changing model and offer together obscures their separate effects.
example: Compare two offer policies separately from asking whether M2 ranks churn risk better than M1.
takeaway: Prediction accuracy and the effect of contacting a customer are different targets.
